SEASON SUMMARY: Freeman only played in 13 games this season, but scored almost 28 points per game, which is frankly ridiculous. He obviously benefitted from Northampton's system, with 16 tries (2nd overall), 33 clean breaks (1st overall) and 1,110 metres made (1st overall). He doesn't even take kicks, and still finished 35 points ahead of 2nd placed Marcus Smith, who does. In fact, Freeman's running and scoring were so good that he finished around 60 points ahead of Kalaveti Ravouvou (the next highest non-kick-taker), who played in 4 more games than Freeman. He will be hard to pass up in 26/27 drafts.

Smith managed over 21 points per game this season in 15 games, and with just one week where he scored more than 40 points, he was reliably good, which helps with fantasy peace of mind. As a FH, his value was anchored by his kicking, although he ranked only 6th among Fly Halves in kicking metrics. This points to his far superior stats for metres made, line breaks and defenders beaten than others at his position. Charlie Atkinson was the only FH better than Smith with the ball, but Atkinson lacks Smith's consistency and kicking volume. One of either Fin or Marcus Smith should be the first FH off the draft board next season - and you'd be very happy with either.

Fin missed the Grand Final and played just 12 games this season (around 300 fewer minutes than #1 FH Marcus Smith), but averaged 29 points per game over Rounds 12-17 to fly up the scoring table and into fantasy managers' hearts. A close second to Marcus atop the Fly Half rankings, Fin profiles slightly differently: while Marcus makes more headway running with the ball and beating defenders, Fin leads all FHs in assists, offloads and conversions. He also made more tackles than any FH other than Harvey Skinner, and concedes noticeably fewer turnovers than other leading 10s.

Ravouvou never had the spike weeks of Freeman or Caluori, but was in the fantasy MVP discussion for most of the season due to ruthless consistency. Wherever you drafted him, he will have paid handsome dividends for a number of reasons: he played in every game other than the Grand Final, averaged almost 18 points per game without many dud weeks, and he's also officially listed as a Centre despite being deployed mostly on the wing. Ravouvou owners essentially had a fourth elite OB every week this season. He didn't really struggle for production later in the season (even though Bristol were a bit of a mess), but he did pick up a couple of yellow cards and conceded a few penalties to dampen his fantasy scores. Ravouvou scored 12 tries, and ranked second out of all players in metres carried and defenders beaten this season.

The Prem is losing one of the most dominant fantasy assets to France next season, so this review is more of a guard of honour than actionable advice. Willis played every single round, and averaged 16.56 points per game. He scored above the average for a Loose Forward in all but 2 games (one of those due to injury). He beat significantly more defenders than anyone else in the league (1-2 more per game than the likes of Ravouvou, O'Flaherty and Feyi-Waboso), led the league in offloads and turnovers won, and for all his work at the breakdown, conceded just 6 penalties. He will have been an absolute cornerstone of fantasy lineups this season, but sadly he is now dead to us, per RFU instructions.

Slade was a great pick at Centre this year - by far the leading true Centre in the league (I'm convinved Ravouvou's listing as a C was an administrative error). Playing 17 games, he averaged over 20 PPG for the first 8 rounds, then had a blip of just 2 PPG for the next 4 rounds, before closing out the season strongly, including a potentially league-winning 34.16 in the Grand Final. Slade's scores were supercharged by his league-leading 17 penalties kicked (as well as taking conversions), and he also scored 8 tries. If you managed to pair Slade at C with a kicking FH, oh boy, that's a recipe for success.

O'Flaherty was not even the leading OB at Sale according to most pre-season predictions, let alone the 2nd top scoring OB overall - he has outperformed expectations in a spectacular way. After a mixed start to the season, he was available as a Free Agent in a lot of leagues from +/- Round 6, and if you picked him up at that point, you were in the money. O'Flaherty rewarded owners with 12 tries (3rd most in the league), 60 defenders beaten (3rd most), and 1,012 metres carried (4th most). He did concede around 20 more turnovers than most other elite players though, with 37 (vs Freeman's 18, Ravouvou's 17 and Willis' 16), but that wouldn't have changed his fantasy outcome much. All in all a great fantasy season!

Despite his 8th place fantasy finish with over 19 points per game, this was a disjointed season for Feyi-Waboso, by his own sky-high standards. His scorching first few rounds gave way to injury and some frustratingly low scores for fantasy managers who had come to rely on him. In fact without his 50 point game in round 14 vs Gloucester (a game Exeter didn't even win), he'd sit 23rd in the fantasy rankings, just below Chiefs teammate Olly Woodburn. Still, Feyi-Waboso passes the eye test maybe more than anyone in the league - he's fun to watch, fun to own and always a scoring threat. He'll be an elite fantasy asset next season.

Arundell is another frustrating fantasy superstar. He legitimately earned his status as a must-start and an MVP candidate over the first 6 rounds (24+ PPG average), before missing a few games and dropping some stinkers. Without his freak 61.52 point day against Newcastle (in the playoffs, so extra brownie points), Arundell would rank 27th rather than 9th. That's not to say 60 point performances from Arundell are so surprising - we're actually disappointed he didn't do that sort of thing more often. The man is clearly rapid, talented and perfectly capable of being your flagship OB in fantasy next season, especially if he can find more consistency.

Hmmm. Caluori makes the top 10 based on total points scored this season, and at 19.82 points per game, he would seem worth it... if you take those stats in isolation. In reality, 72% of his points came in just 3 games - leaving fantasy managers agonising over whether to bench him and risk him scoring 5 tries (which he did twice, both times against Sale), or start him and watch him look absolutely majestic under the high ball without troubling the fantasy scoring elves. In our opinion, despite being a physical freak and obviously unstoppable in some games, Caluori is not a top 10 fantasy asset unless he can demonstrate far more consistency.

Atkinson did not go unnoticed this season by any means, but he still might not be getting enough credit for his fantasy exploits. He ranked 1st among FHs for metres, line breaks, defenders beaten and offloads. He would have also had far more kicking points if Ross Byrne hadn't been on kicking duties for most of the season. In with a genuine shout of being the top FH next season (bold call!) if he cuts out his turnovers, penalties and missed tackles.

Lots of tries, assists, line breaks and metres - Hendy slowed down towards the end of the season fantasy-wise as all the points Northampton were scoring seemed to go to team mates (that ridiculous Bristol game aside). 17.57 PPG is always worth a pick.
Burke ranked top-5 at the FH position in most attacking categories this season gone, and the only thing that hurt him really was losing out to Owen Farrell on kicking duties.

Radwan had a lot of excellent fantasy weeks, some solid but unspectacular weeks, and then scored -0.44 in the Grand Final. Thanks Adam. 15.10 PPG is good and he is clearly talented, so should be looked at in drafts

A selection nightmare, alternating runs of great form with periods of uselessness. Led all OBs in assists and offloads, but missed a lot of tackles and conceded turnovers. Over 13 PPG when playing all 18 games seems like good consistency, and while it's not as bad as some, he could as easily have ruined your season as made it.

Ford's attacking metrics are all noticeably below where we'd expect for FH #5, but his kicking and defensive game means he has a floor of almost 10 PPG before having to do anything special - which he occasionally does. Kicking stats tend not to fade as easily with age either, which is nice.
Only played 10 games, but 23.13 PPG somewhat justifies the hype around this man. Obviously his points all pretty much come from running with the ball. If he's playing, you'll want to start him.

Dombrandt scored just 1 PPG fewer than Tom Willis (although he did play 3 fewer games), scored and assisted more than Willis and basically matched him in every other stat other than defenders beaten (where Willis is a freak). But the best thing about Dombrandt is that you'll actually be able to have him in your team this coming season.

Searle ends the season as the 6th best fantasy FH, but if not for injury that would likely be slightly higher. Searle has a relatively high floor thanks to kicking volume, but also chips in with assists and metres on the ground.

Harding was the joint leading try scorer among forwards in the league, and made 227 tackles (over 14 per game). Only Sale's Ben Bamber made more, but he played 2 more games than Harding. Harding's scoring and tackle-based scoring floor were pretty nice for his owners this season.

Pollock played slightly fewer games than the other elite LFs in '25/26, but his per-game metrics show his value: 1st among LFs in metres and line breaks per game, scored a try every other game and beat 2-3 defenders each week. You'll still draft him (or not) for his personality mainly though.

Got his England call up and had a solid season in general, with one massive week of fantasy scoring. His performances were better in real life than fantasy scoring gave him credit for. His new found international status should give him a confidence boost, but will also cause him to miss more games potentially.

Genuinely sad for how this panned out. 19 year-old Todaro was abolsutely killing it for the first ten games of this season, topping 18 PPG scoring tries and running hard. But an ACL tear picked up on Italy duty ended his season. Northampton didn't need him in the end, but I'd wager Italy could've beaten Ireland (as well as England and Scotland) in the Six Nations if he had been involved. We are not sure when he will return to action.

Loader missed a load of games in the middle of the season - a spell during which most people who drafted him released him into the wild - but picked it up again towards the end of the season, running and hitting with some violence. If he keeps that up he should be good for some points next season.
